title: Harnesses in AI: A Deep Dive — Tejas Kumar, IBM

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's primary focus is agent harness architecture—loops, guardrails, verify steps, context management, and the control plane surrounding a black-box model. The harness engineering concepts are cross-domain and applicable to any agent use case rather than a specific vertical. The talk covers designing an agent harness from first principles and iteratively developing it through a live coding demo. Requires familiarity with agent loops and LLM tool calling but is presented as an accessible deep dive with live coding. An 18-minute conference presentation at AI Engineer with a live coding demo. All evidence anchors are directly sourced from the transcript with said_in_transcript grade.

summary: Tejas Kumar opens by establishing his background at IBM and framing the talk around AI harnesses, a term used loosely across the industry. He notes that in ML a harness is a glorified test suite, but in AI engineering it refers to the infrastructure surrounding an agent's model. The motivation is reliability: most engineers rent inference as a black box with limited context windows and no guarantees about which model is actually served, so harness engineering is the lever they control. He defines an agent harness as 'everything around the model that gives it grounding in reality,' anchoring it with analogies to mountain-climbing harnesses and dog leashes. He enumerates typical components: a tool registry, a model, context management primitives, guardrails, an agent loop, and a verify step. The demo builds a browser-use agent using Playwright and OpenAI's SDK to upvote the first Hacker News post, deliberately using GPT-3.5 Turbo to show that good harness engineering can make a weak model reliable. The initial run fails: the agent hits a login screen, panics, crashes, and lies about success. Tejas refuses to fix this by changing the prompt, instead layering a harness. The first increment adds guardrails: max iterations (six steps) and max messages triggering a naive context compressor that keeps the system prompt, user prompt, and last two messages while removing everything in between. Next, he refactors the code into a formal harness module with a runHarness entry point. Then he adds a deterministic verify step—verify_successful_upvote—that inspects the tool-call history to confirm an actual browser click on the upvote occurred, and catches failed logins and unrecovered login redirects, preventing the agent from lying. A max_attempts guardrail (three tries) is enforced at the harness level. With the verify step, the agent still fails but stops lying. Finally, a login handler runs each agent loop iteration before pushing traces, checks the browser URL, and if on a login page, programmatically injects credentials and submits the form from the harness (not the agent), then adds a message telling the agent login succeeded. The final demo succeeds: the agent opens Hacker News, the harness logs in, the agent upvotes, and closes—succeeding after six iterations. Tejas emphasizes he never touched the prompt. He mentions IBM's open-source open rag project for enterprise RAG with harness-level security. He predicts 2025 was the year of agents, 2026 the year of harnesses, and hopes 2027 brings dynamic on-the-fly generated harnesses where agents create their own guardrails before performing tasks.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: An agent harness is everything around the model that gives it grounding in reality—not the agent loop itself, but the infrastructure surrounding it.
Harness engineering is the primary lever for reliability because most engineers rent black-box models they cannot control or verify.
Key harness components: tool registry, model, context management, guardrails, agent loop, and verify step.
Agent failures (panicking, lying about success) are often harness problems, not prompt problems—the demo fixes everything without touching the prompt.
A verify step that deterministically inspects tool-call history is essential to catch agents lying about what they did.
A login handler that checks the browser URL each loop and injects credentials programmatically from the harness (not the agent) solves authentication barriers securely and deterministically.
Context compression can be naive yet effective: keep the system prompt, user prompt, and last two messages, removing everything in between.
Using an intentionally weak model (GPT-3.5 Turbo) demonstrates that harness engineering can significantly improve agent reliability.
The future may involve dynamic on-the-fly generated harnesses where agents create their own guardrails before performing tasks.
IBM's open-source open rag project uses harness engineering for enterprise-level security in RAG operations on sensitive data.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Tejas Kumar introduces himself as an AI developer advocate at IBM, where they train frontier models and build harnesses. He frames the talk around AI harnesses and polls the audience's confidence on the topic, noting the term means different things in ML vs AI engineering.

sections.title: Why Harness: Reliability and Control
sections.summary: Explains that most engineers rent inference as a black box with limited context windows and no guarantees about which model is served. The name of the game with harnesses is reliability—ensuring agents do what they should irrespective of the black-box model.

sections.title: Defining an Agent Harness from First Principles
sections.summary: Uses mountain-climbing and dog-leash analogies to explain harnesses as anchors to something stable. Distinguishes ML harnesses (test suites) from AI engineering agent harnesses, defining the latter as everything around the model that gives it grounding in reality.

sections.title: Key Components of an Agent Harness
sections.summary: Enumerates typical harness components: tool registry (file system, bash execution), model selection, context management primitives (context compaction), guardrails (max steps), agent loop (possibly a loop around the agent loop), and a verify step (e.g., lint, tests).

sections.title: Demo Setup: Browser Agent on GPT-3.5 Turbo
sections.summary: Introduces the demo: a browser-use agent to upvote the first Hacker News post using GPT-3.5 Turbo intentionally. Shows the project structure with Playwright browser sessions, OpenAI SDK tool definitions, a basic system prompt, and a while-true agent loop that collects events until the LLM says stop.

sections.title: Initial Demo Failure: Login Panic and Lying
sections.summary: The first run opens Hacker News, clicks upvote, hits a login screen, panics, crashes, and then lies about success without verifying. Tejas explicitly rejects fixing this by changing the prompt, framing it as a harness problem.

sections.title: Adding Guardrails to the Harness
sections.summary: First harness increment: adds guardrails with max iterations (six steps) and max messages triggering context compression. These guardrails are applied inside the agent loop, trimming context when message count exceeds the limit.

sections.title: Context Compressor Details and Refactoring into a Formal Harness
sections.summary: Details the naive context compressor: keeps system prompt, user prompt, and last two messages, removing everything in between. Tejas acknowledges this is basic. Then refactors all logic from index.ts into a harness module with a runHarness entry point, reducing the entry point to ~19 lines. The harness does the same work, just encapsulated.

sections.title: Implementing a Verify Step to Catch Lies
sections.summary: Adds a verify step (verify_successful_upvote) as a third argument to runHarness, along with max_attempts (three tries) at the harness level. The verify function deterministically inspects tool-call history for an actual successful browser click on the upvote, and returns early with failure for detected failed logins or unrecovered login redirects. Running with the verify step, the agent still fails but stops lying—the harness catches the false success claim by checking tool history.

sections.title: Implementing a Login Handler for Programmatic Access
sections.summary: Adds createLoginHandler, which runs each agent loop iteration before pushing traces. It checks the browser session's current URL; if not on a login page, it does nothing (computationally cheap). If on a login page, it programmatically fills credentials and submits the form from the harness—not the agent—deterministically and securely. It pushes a message into the queue: 'I'm the harness. I logged in. You're good now.'

sections.title: Final Demonstration: Successful Autonomous Upvoting
sections.summary: The final run: the agent opens Hacker News, hits the login page, the harness logs in programmatically, the agent upvotes the first post, and closes. Succeeds after six iterations. Tejas verifies on Hacker News that the upvote actually occurred.

sections.title: Summary and the Future of Dynamic Harnesses
sections.summary: Tejas emphasizes he never touched the prompt—only built a harness, and the outcome radically changed. Harnesses matter because models are non-deterministic and you want to use cheap models with great harnesses. Mentions IBM's open-source open rag project for enterprise RAG with harness-level security. Predicts 2025 was the year of agents, 2026 the year of harnesses, and hopes 2027 brings dynamic on-the-fly generated harnesses where agents self-create guardrails before performing tasks—a step toward AGI.
